summaries.example: Imagine that Maya thinks eating meat is wrong, while Leo thinks it is allowed. They are not just choosing different snacks. They disagree about what people ought to do. Their disagreement might come from different ideas about animals, health, or fairness. Philosophers ask whether their beliefs are clashing facts, or whether their feelings and choices are pulling in opposite directions.
summaries.summary: People often disagree about what is right and wrong, both within communities and across cultures. Philosophers ask what this disagreement really is. A moral realist may say that people hold opposite beliefs about one truth, much as they can disagree about a fact. A non-cognitivist may instead say that moral judgments express feelings, desires, or plans, so disagreement is a clash of attitudes. Relativists offer views in which moral truth depends in some way on standards or assessors. The entry also considers especially deep disagreements that might remain even under very good conditions. Such disagreement has been used to question moral realism, but realists reply that disputes may result from different non-moral facts, bias, self-interest, or limited reflection. The main lesson is that disagreement matters, but it does not settle the debate by itself.
key_ideas: People and societies disagree about many moral questions.
Some philosophers understand moral disagreement as conflicting beliefs about truth.
Others understand it as a clash of feelings, desires, or attitudes.
Disagreement may come from missing facts, bias, self-interest, or different life experiences.
Philosophers debate whether disagreement challenges the idea of objective moral truths.
summaries.why_it_matters: Learning about moral disagreement can help us listen carefully without assuming that every disagreement has a simple explanation. It also shows why philosophers ask what words such as “right” and “wrong” mean, how we can know moral truths, and whether moral questions work like scientific questions. Studying these possibilities encourages respectful discussion and more careful thinking.

important_terms.definition: A disagreement about what is right, wrong, good, or bad.
The view that some moral truths are real and do not depend only on what people or groups think.
The view that moral judgments may depend on a person’s or group’s standards or point of view.
A belief or feeling that pushes someone toward or away from an action.
A disagreement that would continue even after people had excellent information and careful thinking.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people disagree because they have different facts rather than different moral values?
If many thoughtful people disagree, should everyone become less certain?
Could a disagreement be real even if the people’s feelings, rather than their beliefs, are in conflict?
Are moral questions different from questions in science or mathematics?

summaries.example: Suppose two well-informed ethicists disagree about whether a severe punishment is morally justified. They share many facts and understand each other’s arguments, yet their disagreement remains. One philosopher might treat their claims as incompatible beliefs: at most one can be correct. A non-cognitivist might analyze the dispute as opposing practical attitudes toward punishment. A relativist might say that the claims are true relative to different standards, although some relativist theories preserve a shared proposition whose truth varies with an assessor’s standards. The case raises questions about knowledge, meaning, and whether the disagreement is genuinely radical.
summaries.summary: The existence of widespread moral disagreement has been important in metaethics because it bears on moral reality, knowledge, and language. On a cognitivist realist account, disagreement is a conflict between beliefs that assign incompatible verdicts to the same truth-evaluable claim. Non-cognitivists instead analyze moral opposition as a clash of conative attitudes, such as desires or commitments. Relativist cognitivists allow moral truth conditions to vary with standards, speakers, or assessors, though some versions preserve a common proposition and a genuine dispute. The strongest challenge concerns radical disagreement: disagreement that would survive ideal inquiry. Realists can respond that many disputes depend on non-moral facts, evidence, bias, self-interest, or limited reflection, and that convergence may still occur. Other arguments claim that disagreement threatens moral knowledge through peer disagreement, unsafe belief-forming methods, or even merely possible disagreement. The entry also examines how disagreement affects theories of moral meaning, including debates about reference and the Moral Twin Earth case. None of these arguments is decisive in isolation, and attempts to draw skeptical conclusions must avoid extending the same reasoning too readily to every domain.
key_ideas: The philosophical significance of disagreement depends partly on what counts as disagreement: incompatible beliefs or clashing practical attitudes.
Moral disagreement can be used in arguments for relativism, non-cognitivism, skepticism, or anti-realism, but it has also been used to motivate realist responses.
Realists may explain disagreement through factual differences, bias, self-interest, inadequate evidence, or insufficient reflection.
A radical disagreement is more challenging than one caused by ordinary mistakes, but it is difficult to establish that actual disagreements meet this standard.
Epistemological arguments focus on whether disagreement undermines justification or knowledge, including arguments from peer disagreement and safety.
Arguments from moral disagreement face over-generalization and self-defeat worries if similar reasoning applies to science, mathematics, or epistemology.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moral disagreement connects abstract questions to everyday reasoning. It asks whether being outnumbered matters, whether competent disagreement should change one’s confidence, and what makes a dispute genuinely about the same issue. The debate also illustrates a broader philosophical method: evidence rarely supports a conclusion without additional assumptions about truth, justification, language, or explanation. Understanding those assumptions makes moral arguments more precise and helps distinguish disagreement about values from disagreement about facts.

important_terms.definition: The area of philosophy that studies what moral facts are, how moral claims can be known, and what moral language means.
The view that moral claims express beliefs that can be true or false.
The view that moral claims do not primarily report truth-apt beliefs, but express attitudes such as approval, disapproval, or desire.
The view that there are moral truths or properties independent of human practices and thinking.
The view that moral truth conditions or standards vary with speakers, groups, contexts, or assessors.
A disagreement that would persist in ideal conditions, after relevant factual and cognitive obstacles were removed.
The idea that a belief could not easily have been false when formed by the same method; some theories treat this as required for knowledge.
A theory of meaning or reference that interprets speakers in a way that makes many of their claims come out true.

questions_to_think_about: Does widespread disagreement provide evidence against objective moral truths, or only against our ability to know them?
What would count as an ideal condition for moral inquiry?
Should learning that an equally capable thinker disagrees reduce your confidence, or can you reasonably remain steadfast?
Can a realist explain genuine disagreement when different communities use moral terms according to very different standards?
When does an argument from disagreement over-generalize to other fields?

summaries.example: Two student councils are deciding whether students should be allowed to use phones during lunch. One group says it is unfair because some students cannot afford phones and because phones can exclude people. Another group says students should be free to choose how to spend their break. They may disagree about the moral rule, but they may also disagree about facts, such as whether phone use really harms conversation. Philosophers ask whether the disagreement is about one shared truth, different standards, or opposing attitudes and plans.
summaries.summary: Moral disagreement occurs when people or groups give opposing answers to questions about right, wrong, good, or bad. The difficult philosophical question is what “opposing” means. Cognitivists regard moral judgments as beliefs that can be true or false, so disagreement resembles a conflict about facts. Non-cognitivists understand moral judgments more like desires, approvals, or commitments, making disagreement a clash of practical attitudes. Relativists hold that moral truth may depend on standards, social groups, or assessors; some versions still preserve a common subject matter and genuine opposition. Philosophers often focus on radical disagreement, which would remain even when people have good evidence and reason carefully. Realists argue that many actual disputes are explained by different factual assumptions, bias, self-interest, or insufficient reflection. Critics reply that persistent disagreement may create problems for moral knowledge or for the claim that moral truths are objective. The entry presents several arguments and responses, while emphasizing that disagreement alone does not determine which metaethical theory is correct.
key_ideas: Moral disagreements are widespread, but philosophers disagree about what makes opposing moral convictions genuinely opposed.
Realists usually treat moral disagreement as incompatible beliefs about a truth; non-cognitivists may treat it as conflicting attitudes or action-guiding commitments.
Relativist theories can make moral truth depend on standards while offering different accounts of whether people with different standards genuinely disagree.
Some disagreements are caused by different beliefs about consequences or other non-moral facts.
Arguments against moral realism often focus on disagreement that would survive careful inquiry, but showing that a disagreement is radical is difficult.
Disagreement can create skeptical worries, especially when equally capable people hold opposing views, yet those worries may be limited rather than global.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moral disagreement affects how we debate difficult issues and how confident we should be in our own judgments. It teaches that a disagreement may involve facts, meanings, standards, emotions, or beliefs about truth. Examining these possibilities can make conversations less hostile and arguments more careful. It also introduces an important philosophical habit: asking what extra assumptions are needed before evidence supports a large conclusion.

important_terms.definition: A disagreement about what people ought to do or what is morally right or wrong.
The philosophical study of moral truth, knowledge, and the meaning of moral language.
The position that moral statements express beliefs that can be true or false.
The position that moral statements mainly express attitudes, commitments, or desires rather than ordinary factual beliefs.
The view that moral truth is independent of what humans happen to believe or practice.
The view that moral judgments depend on standards connected with people, groups, contexts, or assessors.
A disagreement that would remain even under conditions with excellent evidence and careful reasoning.
A thinker who is about as well placed as you are to reach the truth about a particular kind of question.

questions_to_think_about: If two people use different moral standards, are they disagreeing about the same thing?
How can we tell whether a disagreement comes from moral principles or from different factual beliefs?
Should discovering an epistemic peer’s opposing view change your confidence?
Why might philosophers give special attention to disagreements that continue after careful reflection?
Would an argument based on moral disagreement also challenge disagreement in science or mathematics?
